name: Kwalhioqua-Clatskanie
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Only wordlists exist (Hale 1846; Boas & Goddard 1924 IJAL vocabulary); no grammar or phonology of Kwalhioqua-Clatskanie is attested.

new_statements.quote: For Kwalhioqua-Tlatskanai a careful study of the many accent marks in the sources reveals a very different pattern from that in the Tsetsaut. Here the stress generally appears on the stem-vowel if full, constricted or not [...]. With reduced stem vowel and reduced suffixes, constricted or not, the accent marks are so random that they clearly imply only virtual monotone [...]. It therefore seems highly unlikely that Kwalhioqua-Tlatskanai had any tone, but rather that it had strong stress on full vowels, and some subsidiary rules, some of the details of which can probably be figured out, as in the case of the PCA and other toneless languages, including Babine-Hagwilgate.
new_statements.citation: Krauss, Michael E. 2005 [1979]. Athabaskan Tone (1979). In Sharon Hargus & Keren Rice (eds.), Athabaskan Prosody (Current Issues in Linguistic Theory 269), 55-136. Amsterdam: John Benjamins. doi:10.1075/cilt.269.07kra. [Read in the ANLA 2003 typeset of the October 1979 typescript, ANLA CA961K1978.]
new_statements.locator: Sec. 7.1 'Extinct Athabaskan', pp. 60-61 of the ANLA 2003 typeset (krauss-1979-tone(2003).pdf); corresponding passage in the 2005 Benjamins printing within pp. 55-136
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (72 pp., Quartz PDF created 2003-08-12; title page 'ATHABASKAN TONE / MICHAEL KRAUSS / Alaska Native Language Center / October, 1979') and its text dump lines 2400-2422). The quoted passage sits exactly where the report says: sec. 7 'Less understood languages', 7.1 'Extinct Athabaskan', beginning on typeset p. 60 (PDF page 60, running head '60 MICHAEL KRAUSS') and running onto p. 61 ('ATHABASKAN TONE 61'). Word-for-word match: 'For Kwalhioqua-Tlatskanai a careful study of the many accent marks in the sources reveals a very different pattern from that in the Tsetsaut. Here the stress generally appears on the stem-vowel if full, constricted or not, transcriptions usually implyin…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No tone. Stress (as inferred philologically from the accent marks of the 1841-1910 transcribers) falls on the noun/verb stem syllable when the stem vowel is a full vowel, whether or not the syllable is constricted (glottalized), e.g. [w´ta@&] 'his father', [w´ga@>ne&] 'his arm' with prefix unstressed and stem stressed; when the stem vowel is reduced (and suffixes reduced) no consistent stress is recoverable ('virtual monotone'). I.e. stem-based, vowel-quality(full vs reduced)-conditioned stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated; Krauss only alludes to 'some subsidiary rules' not yet worked out.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with reduced stem vowels show random accent placement in the sources (e.g. the several transcriptions of 'ear', 'younger brother', 'child'), interpreted as near-monotone rather than a different stress rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Inference from accent marks on isolated citation forms (mostly possessed nouns) in eight amateur wordlists; word-level; Krauss frames it as strong stress on full (stem) vowels in a toneless language, by analogy with Pacific Coast Athabaskan and Babine-Hagwilgate.
new_statements.identity_note: Krauss treats Kwalhioqua (Washington side) and Tlatskanai/Clatskanie (Oregon side) as 'very close if not identical' dialects of one language with no systematic differences in the corpus; the statement covers both, i.e. glottocode kwal1258 as a whole. The stress pattern is a philological reconstruction from accent marks in eight pre-1911 amateur wordlists (Hale, Anderson, Gibbs, Boas, Wickersham, Curtis/Myers, Teit, Frachtenberg), not from fieldwork with speakers.

sources.citation: Krauss, Michael E. 1979/2005. Athabaskan Tone. Typescript, Alaska Native Language Center, October 1979 (ANLA CA961K1978, 2003 typeset version); published as 'Athabaskan Tone (1979)' in S. Hargus & K. Rice (eds.), Athabaskan Prosody (CILT 269), Amsterdam: Benjamins, 55-136, doi:10.1075/cilt.269.07kra.
sources.note: Sec. 7.1 (pp. 60-61 of the ANLA typeset): from a study of the accent marks in all K-T sources, stress generally falls on the stem vowel if it is a full vowel (constricted or not); with reduced stem vowels and reduced suffixes the accent marks are random, implying virtual monotone; concludes K-T had no tone but 'strong stress on full vowels, and some subsidiary rules'; lists K-T among the definitely toneless Athabaskan languages.
